questions.q: In the standard try/Assert.fail()/catch pattern for testing exceptions, what is the purpose of placing Assert.fail() immediately after the call under test inside the try block?
options: It improves code coverage automatically
It forces the test to fail if the expected exception was not actually thrown
It is required syntax for all Apex try blocks
It suppresses the exception so it doesn't propagate
questions.explain: Without Assert.fail() right after the call, a test that expects an exception but silently doesn't get one (because a bug removed the check) would incorrectly pass — Assert.fail() forces that scenario to be caught as a failure.

questions.q: Why is catching the generic Exception type and asserting nothing further considered a weak negative test?
options: Apex does not allow catching the generic Exception type
It would pass equally whether the intended business exception occurred or an unrelated bug threw a completely different exception
It always causes a compilation error
It automatically disables code coverage for that method
questions.explain: A broad catch(Exception e) with no further assertions passes for almost any failure — intended or not — so it doesn't actually prove the specific failure you meant to test for.

questions.q: What exception type is thrown when a DML statement is blocked by a validation rule or an addError() call?
options: QueryException
DmlException
CalloutException
LimitException
questions.explain: Validation rules and addError() calls surface as a DmlException when the triggering DML statement runs, with the error text accessible via getMessage().

questions.q: Why would a test check e.getMessage().contains('Amount cannot be negative') rather than just checking that a DmlException was thrown at all?
options: To prove the specific validation rule fired, not just that the insert failed for some unspecified reason
Because DmlException never actually has a message
Because .contains() is required syntax for all exception handling
To bypass the need for an insert statement
questions.explain: Checking for a distinctive piece of the validation rule's own error text confirms the right rule actually blocked the record, rather than some other unrelated validation failure.

questions.q: What is the benefit of defining a custom exception class like 'public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {}' instead of always throwing a generic Exception?
options: It automatically increases code coverage
It lets calling code and tests catch exactly the specific failure they care about, without accidentally swallowing unrelated bugs
Custom exceptions run faster than built-in exceptions
It removes the need for any assertions in the catch block
questions.explain: A named, specific exception type lets both production code and tests target exactly the failure they intend to handle, rather than broadly catching Exception and potentially masking unrelated bugs.
